newsitem.title: USA: Tough negotiations ahead on taxes, spending cuts.
newsitem.headline: Tough negotiations ahead on taxes, spending cuts.

text.p: Lawmakers rushed to congratulate themselves on passage in the House and Senate of budget and tax cut bills last week, but a summer of long, heated battles was expected before they become law.

"We indeed made history. We passed a package that balances the budget while offering Americans the first tax cut in 16 years. And we passed it in a bipartisan way," Senate Finance Committee Chairman William Roth of Delaware said immediately after the Senate passed the tax bill.

While lawmakers joined hands in the Senate to pass the tax and spending cut bills, Democrats rebelled in the House despite urging from President Clinton to support the spending plans. He did not ask for their votes on the tax bill.

Just two years ago, the Republican-led Congress and the White House were headed into a budget battle that resulted in two unpopular shutdowns of government agencies and threatened the delay of government checks for the elderly and needy.
When Congress returns July 7 from a brief Independence Day recess, House and Senate lawmakers will begin meeting jointly to iron out differences in their versions of the two bills.

The negotiations will become a delicate balancing act for congressional leaders and the White House. Republicans, particularly House Speaker Newt Gingrich who had to quell a conservative rebellion this month, cannot move too far into Clinton's camp. Yet, they cannot risk a veto by the president.
This time, as Republican leaders in the House pointed out, the White House will sit with them at the negotiating table to reach an agreement Clinton will sign into law.

"We're going to work with the president and his team," Gingrich told reporters at a news conference Thursday. Jubiliant Republican House leaders sported bright smiley-face stickers on their lapels to celebrate passage of the tax bill.
"I think we can come to agreement on the final package as adults," House Republican Conference Chairman John Boehner of Ohio told reporters.

Still, as the Senate debated its tax bill Friday, Clinton sent word that he found both the House and Senate tax bills unacceptable and would Monday outline what he wanted to see in the final tax package.
"The president wants a tax cut. He wants a targeted tax cut, and the House and Senate measures don't quite muster up at this point," White House spokesman Mike McCurry said.

One of the most politically sensitive issues facing Clinton is a Senate plan to make wealthier elderly pay more for Medicare and raise the eligibility age gradually to 67 from 65. Democrats are split on the issue with House Democrats strongly opposed and House Republicans are waiting for a signal from Clinton before they back the controversial idea.

On the tax bill, Clinton has said it did not go far enough to provide the middle class with education and child tax credits and he strongly objects to indexing for inflation a cut in the capital gains tax rate.
The Senate tax plan provides $77 billion of tax cuts over five years and the House version $85 billion -- the larger amount being the one agreed to by budget negotiators in May.
While the budget and tax package, based on current economic forecasts, would bring the deficit to zero by 2002, there were lawmakers who remained sceptical.

Sen. Dale Bumpers, an Arkansas Democrat, warned that tax cuts will add to the deficit. "When the year 2002 rolls around we will not have a balanced budget or anything close to it ... Today we just forsook the opportunity," to balance the budget, he said after the Senate's tax vote.
